answer_text:
Let

\[
a_{n,k}=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\cos\sqrt{k/n}}{2^k}, & 0\le k\le n,\\[4pt]
0, & k>n.
\end{cases}
\]

Then the given sum is

\[
\sum_{k=0}^n \frac{\cos\sqrt{k/n}}{2^k}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_{n,k}.
\]

For each fixed \(k\), as \(n\to\infty\),

\[
\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}\to 0,
\]

so

\[
\cos\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}\to 1.
\]

Thus

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty} a_{n,k}=\frac{1}{2^k}.
\]

Also, for all \(n,k\),

\[
|a_{n,k}|\le \frac{1}{2^k},
\]

and

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^k}=2<\infty.
\]

Therefore we may pass the limit inside the infinite sum by dominated convergence (or the Weierstrass M-test):

\[
I=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{n,k}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}a_{n,k}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^k}.
\]

The geometric series gives

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^k}=2.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{2}
\]

27B·v4.method: Pointwise convergence of each term plus dominated convergence (geometric tail bound) to interchange limit and sum, yielding the geometric series sum 2.
